newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Ethnic tensions rising across Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Ethnic tensions rising across Bosnia.

text.p: The United Nations said on Thursday that tensions were rising in Bosnia, with ethnic-based arrests and destruction of homes reported in the northwest and south of the country.

Five Moslem houses were set on fire on Wednesday while a group of 80 Moslems were visiting their former village Bivolje Brdo, south of the city of Mostar, which is now controlled by Croats, a U.N. spokeswoman said.
An aggressive crowd of 20 Croats was waiting for the Moslems' bus and forced them to leave ahead of schedule, said Ariane Quentier, spokeswoman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
"This incident falls in a series of incidents that occured in Mostar," she told reporters.
Although Bosnian Moslems and Croats have lived in an uneasy U.S.-brokered federation since 1994, when they ended an 11-month war, international efforts have failed to reconcile them.
Moslem-Croat divisions are most bitterly felt in Mostar, devastated by fighting, where a European Union administration has tried to create joint institutions and a unified police.
Quentier said Mostar Croats were obstructing a pilot project aiming to return 70 families to each sector of the city.
"They simply did not show up for the last meeting on Monday," she said.
Moslems and Serbs were also involved in incidents in the northwest of Bosnia, the United Nations said.

Three days ago six Serbs were beaten up while visiting the Moslem town of Sanski Most using a UNHCR-sponsored bus line set up to encourage visits between the two deeply divided communities, Quentier said.
That incident was followed by the arrest of a Serb, Milorad Marceta, by Bosnian government police on war crimes charges, U.N. police spokesman Patrik Svensson said.
When Marceta did not return to the Serb town of Prijedor an angry crowd gathered, threatening to detain U.N. monitors.
"After some time the situation calmed down but we are very concerned about this increase of tension," Svensson said.
In retaliation, a Serb crowd gathered again on Wednesday to wait for visiting Moslems and forced them to return, he said.
